source_read: PDF, pp. 1238-1244 (all pages); Table 2 (p. 1240) and Table 3 (p. 1241) checked on rendered pages.

claims.overstatement: None: the claim says 'one laboratory study', names the kit, and states the absence of PMA, MDA and methamphetamine. Two precision points: (1) 'a DanceSafe kit' was two identical kits bought online, neither with a lot number; (2) 'No sample contained PMA, MDA or methamphetamine on its own' is true, but none contained them at all (PMMA and amphetamine, which did occur, are different compounds), so 'on its own' can be dropped.
claims.note: Every Murray number recomputes: 35/35 (Wilson 90.1-100, same), 4/4 (51.0-100, same), 3/4 for analyst 1 (75%; 30.1-95.4); Part II with the three reagents and an 'MDMA-like' reading counted as positive (the paper's stated rule): true positives 2, false negatives 2, false positives 5, true negatives 7, so sensitivity 2/4 = 50%, specificity 7/12 = 58.3%, PPV 2/7 = 28.6% and NPV 7/9 = 77.8% (printed 28% and 77%, truncated rather than rounded); Novice A 0/2 and 5/6, Novice B 2/2 and 2/6; Marquis alone 5 + 5 = 10 false positives of 12 and 2 false negatives. The seven second-drug samples (amphetamine 1, ephedrine or pseudoephedrine 2, PMMA 1, diazepam 1, caffeine 2) were all read positive. Conditions the claim could add: 3-5 mg of scraped powder per test; Part I readers had agreed colour names and practised before testing, which is more than the leaflet a home user gets; readings were recorded in two runs with one analyst observing both, so the three analysts were not fully independent; the paper reports only positive or negative per sample, not the colours (analysts disagreed on exact colours; Marquis-alone Part I results not shown); Part II drugs other than MDMA were pharmaceutical dosage forms. The Table 2 footnote calls the Part I analysts experienced chemists familiar with the reagents, while the abstract calls them experienced toxicologists using an unfamiliar procedure. The limitations anchor's locator was recounted in step 2 as Discussion, 7th paragraph; its page and data are unchanged from the blind reading.

anchors.extracted: Two identical DanceSafe adulterant screening kits were bought online; they had no lot numbers to check consistency. Before testing, three analysts studied the procedure and the kit's colour charts, agreed on colour names, and practised on generic pills.

39 street tablets sold as MDMA and held as evidence (county sheriff's office, university forensic toxicology laboratory) were used because no others were available; analysts picked varied appearances; 3-5 mg of powder scraped from each, with equal aliquots for the colour tests and for full-scan GC-MS.

One analyst tested while a second observed and both recorded independently, a third timed; the first and third then swapped roles and repeated the tests on a randomised set. The Marquis reaction was judged alone, then together with Mecke and Simon's reagents, using the instructions and colour charts.

Each analyst recorded 35 positives; GC-MS found MDMA in all 35; seven of them also held caffeine, ephedrine or pseudoephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA and were read positive like the rest. The four non-MDMA samples (alprazolam; ephedrine or pseudoephedrine with guaifenesin; ephedrine or pseudoephedrine with caffeine; no active principle) were negative for analysts 2 and 3; analyst 1 read the one with no identifiable drug as weakly positive. Marquis-alone results were similar (not shown); analysts disagreed on the exact colours.

Follow-up because the evidence tablets were almost certain to contain MDMA: two testers who were pharmacology and toxicology professionals with no practical experience of such kits received eight blinded samples (codeine, dextromethorphan, dihydrocodeine, ketamine, MDMA twice, morphine, d-norpropoxyphene) and the kit's labelling only, with no other instruction (single-blind).

anchors.locator: Results > Part II, 1st paragraph; Table 3 and footnote a
anchors.extracted: With all three reagents, Novice A called only morphine positive (MDMA-like): 2 false negatives, 1 false positive; Novice B called only ketamine and d-norpropoxyphene negative, both MDMA samples and codeine MDMA, and dextromethorphan, dihydrocodeine and morphine MDMA-like: 4 false positives, no false negative. Counting MDMA-like as positive, sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV printed as 50%, 58%, 28% and 77%. Marquis alone: 5 false positives and 2 false negatives (A), 5 false positives and none (B). A tester was slightly injured by a spilled drop of reagent.

Authors name selection bias and analyst bias, a small sample (39, all that was available), samples from different sources, and Part II drugs that were pharmaceutical dosage forms of known quality (except MDMA) that may react differently from clandestine products.

Authors write that the reagents did not separate pure from adulterated MDMA, lacked sensitivity and specificity with unfamiliar testers, and that experienced toxicologists produced false positives (Part I shows one weak positive by one analyst); they conclude none of the reagents should be used by the public, on two novice testers and eight samples.

claims.note: The Murray sentence is accurate and labelled as a laboratory study of a colour kit. It is indirect for a claim about fentanyl strips used at home: two testers, both pharmacology and toxicology professionals new to the kit, eight pharmaceutical or seized samples, in a laboratory. Both directions recompute: Novice A 2 false negatives (both MDMA) and 1 false positive (morphine), Novice B 4 false positives; with the Marquis reagent alone 10 of 12 non-MDMA readings were positive and 2 of 4 MDMA readings negative.

anchors.extracted: Two testers new to the kit misread known drugs in both directions: Novice A missed both MDMA samples and called morphine MDMA-like; Novice B called four non-MDMA drugs (codeine, dihydrocodeine, dextromethorphan, morphine) MDMA or MDMA-like; with the Marquis reagent alone they gave 10 false positives in 12 non-MDMA readings and 2 false negatives.
The testers were pharmacology and toxicology professionals inexperienced with the kits, working in a laboratory from the kit's labelling alone, on eight blinded samples.

claims.note: 'The same positive MDMA reading' is right as a binary result: the paper reports only positive or negative per sample, not the colours, and says the analysts disagreed on exact colours. 7 of 35 recomputes from Table 2 (amphetamine 1, ephedrine or pseudoephedrine 2, PMMA 1, diazepam 1, caffeine 2). Murray did not measure amount; its only statement on quantity is second-hand (EMCDDA rating the Marquis test non-quantifiable, p. 1242).

anchors.extracted: Seven of the 35 MDMA samples also contained caffeine, ephedrine or pseudoephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA, and every analyst read them positive exactly as the MDMA-only samples (positive or negative only; colours not reported).

Authors conclude the three reagents did not differentiate pure from adulterated MDMA, and cite the EMCDDA rating of the Marquis test as unreliable, non-quantifiable and giving no information about adulterants (second-hand), with which they say their results concur.

key_findings.correction: The text says ephedrine or pseudoephedrine (p. 1241); Table 2 says ephedrine.
Discussion 7th paragraph by my count too.
Refs 30-33 are Jacobs (Med J Aust), a Western Australian teacher resource, Bellis et al. (Addict Behav) and a Glasgow Herald article.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed; note that the abstract does attach the lack of sensitivity and specificity to persons unfamiliar with the reagents, so the issue is the omission of Part I rather than a misattribution.

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with high for sample selection and index test, unclear for the reference standard, and overall high. On flow and timing I would judge low rather than unclear: within each part every sample received the same reference and appears in the analysis, the interval matters little for stable seized material, and the different references in Parts I and II belong to two separate analyses, not to differential verification within one. This does not change the overall judgment.

missed: Cross-source context, not a finding of this paper: the Marquis reagent gives violet with codeine, dihydrocodeine and morphine (Winstock et al., 2001, Table 2, p. 1144; Philp & Fu, 2018, AM p. 4), so the Part II panel (5 of 8 samples opioids or dextromethorphan) was weighted toward known cross-reactants; worth a line where Part II's specificity is cited.
